_link.title: I can describe the flight path of a projectile and explain the effect of gravity on its trajectory

toLevel2.question: A ball is launched into the air. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following best describes the shape of the flight path of the ball?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The combination of constant horizontal velocity and uniformly accelerated vertical motion produces a parabolic trajectory.

distractors.explanation: A straight line would require no acceleration; the gravitational force curves the path into a parabola.
Circular motion requires a centripetal force of constant magnitude; the gravitational force acts only downward, producing a parabola.
Hyperbolic paths occur in certain orbital mechanics scenarios; near-Earth projectiles follow parabolas.

toLevel2.question: A ball is launched as a projectile. Which one of the following best describes the direction in which the gravitational force acts on the ball during its flight?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The gravitational force always acts vertically downward toward the centre of the Earth throughout the entire flight.

distractors.explanation: The gravitational force acts vertically downward, not along the curved trajectory of the projectile.
The gravitational force acts downward regardless of the projectile's direction of travel at any point.
The gravitational force has no horizontal component; it acts only in the vertical direction.

toLevel2.question: A ball is launched as a projectile. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following best describes what happens to the horizontal velocity of the ball during its flight?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: With no horizontal force acting on the projectile, the horizontal velocity stays the same throughout the flight.

distractors.explanation: Without air resistance, no horizontal force acts to decelerate the projectile.
No horizontal force means no horizontal acceleration, so the speed cannot increase.

distractors.answer: It becomes zero at the peak
distractors.explanation: Only the vertical velocity becomes zero at the peak; horizontal velocity is unchanged.

toLevel2.question: A ball is launched at an angle above the horizontal. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following best describes the vertical velocity of the ball at the highest point of its trajectory?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: At the peak, the ball has momentarily stopped moving upward and has not yet begun moving downward, so the vertical velocity is zero.

distractors.explanation: The vertical component decreases as the projectile rises and reaches zero at the peak.
9.8 m s⁻² is the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration, not the velocity at the peak.
The vertical velocity is at its minimum magnitude (zero) at the peak, not its maximum.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is closest to the magnitude and direction of the gravitational acceleration near the surface of Earth?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Near Earth's surface, all objects experience a gravitational acceleration of approximately 9.8 m s⁻² directed downward.

distractors.explanation: The units of acceleration are m s⁻², not m s⁻¹.
Gravitational acceleration is directed downward toward Earth, not upward.
Gravitational acceleration is approximately 9.8 m s⁻² at the surface, not zero.

toLevel2.question: A student claims: 'A projectile follows a parabolic path because the gravitational force acts only in the vertical direction.' The student's claim is correct.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The gravitational force provides a constant downward acceleration while horizontal motion is unaffected, producing the characteristic parabolic shape.

distractors.explanation: Students may think other forces shape the trajectory, but with air resistance ignored, only the vertical gravitational force creates the parabola.

toLevel2.question: A student states: 'At the peak of its trajectory, a projectile has zero acceleration.' The student's statement is correct.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The gravitational force acts on the projectile throughout its flight, including at the peak. The acceleration is always 9.8 m s⁻² downward, even when the vertical velocity is momentarily zero.

distractors.explanation: Students often confuse zero vertical velocity at the peak with zero acceleration, but the gravitational force continues to accelerate the projectile downward.

toLevel2.prompt: A ball is launched into the air. Ignore air resistance. Complete the sentence about the flight of the ball.
toLevel2.sentence: A projectile follows a {{blank:1}} path because the gravitational force accelerates it {{blank:2}} throughout the flight.

1.correctExplanation: The combination of constant horizontal motion and accelerated vertical motion traces out a parabola.

distractors.explanation: Circular paths require centripetal force; projectiles near Earth follow parabolas.
A straight line would require no net force; the gravitational force curves the path.

2.correctExplanation: The gravitational force always acts vertically downward, which is the only acceleration on the projectile.

distractors.explanation: The gravitational force has no component along the horizontal direction of travel.
The gravitational force does not oppose the horizontal motion; it acts vertically downward.

toLevel2.prompt: A ball is launched as a projectile. Ignore air resistance. Complete the sentence about the velocity components of the ball.
toLevel2.sentence: During projectile flight, the {{blank:1}} velocity remains constant while the {{blank:2}} velocity changes due to the gravitational force.

1.correctExplanation: No horizontal force acts on the projectile (ignoring air resistance), so horizontal velocity is constant.

distractors.explanation: Vertical velocity changes continuously because the gravitational force accelerates the projectile downward.
The total speed changes as the vertical component changes; only the horizontal component stays constant.

2.correctExplanation: The gravitational force accelerates the projectile downward at 9.8 m s⁻², continuously changing the vertical velocity.

distractors.explanation: Horizontal velocity stays constant because no horizontal force acts on the projectile.
Angular velocity is not a standard component in projectile motion analysis.

toLevel2.prompt: A ball is launched at an angle above the horizontal. Ignore air resistance. Complete the sentence about the ball at the peak of its trajectory.
toLevel2.sentence: At the highest point, the ball's vertical velocity is {{blank:1}} but the gravitational force still provides an acceleration of {{blank:2}} m s⁻² downward.

1.correctExplanation: The vertical velocity decreases to zero at the peak before the projectile begins falling back down.

distractors.explanation: The vertical velocity is at its minimum magnitude (zero) at the peak, not maximum.
At the exact peak, the vertical velocity is zero; it becomes negative only after the peak.

2.correctExplanation: Gravitational acceleration remains constant at 9.8 m s⁻² throughout the entire flight, including at the peak.

distractors.explanation: The gravitational acceleration does not become zero at the peak; only the vertical velocity is zero.
4.9 is half of 9.8 and appears in displacement equations, but the acceleration is always 9.8 m s⁻².

toLevel3.question: A ball is launched into the air as a projectile. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following best describes why the ball's path curves downward rather than continuing in a straight line after launch?
toLevel3.correct: The gravitational force continuously accelerates the ball downward
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The constant downward gravitational force adds an increasing downward displacement over time, bending the path into a curve.

distractors.answer: The ball runs out of forward momentum
distractors.explanation: Horizontal momentum is conserved; the curve is caused by the gravitational force, not loss of forward motion.

distractors.answer: Air resistance pushes the ball downward
distractors.explanation: Air resistance is ignored in this scenario. The gravitational force alone causes the fundamental parabolic curve.

distractors.answer: The launch force wears off during the flight
distractors.explanation: Once launched, no launch force acts on the projectile; the gravitational force alone curves the path.

toLevel3.question: A ball is launched at an angle above the horizontal. Ignore air resistance. At the peak of the trajectory, the vertical velocity is zero. Which one of the following best describes why the ball does not remain stationary at the peak?
toLevel3.correct: The gravitational force continues to accelerate the ball downward from that point
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Although the vertical velocity is momentarily zero, the constant downward acceleration immediately begins increasing the downward velocity.

distractors.answer: Horizontal velocity pushes the ball past the peak
distractors.explanation: Horizontal motion continues but does not explain why the ball descends; the gravitational force causes the descent.

distractors.answer: The ball stores energy that is released at the peak
distractors.explanation: No energy is stored and released at the peak; the gravitational force acts continuously.

distractors.answer: Air pressure forces the ball back downward
distractors.explanation: Air pressure does not push projectiles down; the gravitational acceleration is responsible.

toLevel3.question: Sam launches one ball horizontally from the edge of a cliff and another ball at an angle above the horizontal from the same height. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following best describes how the trajectory of the horizontally launched ball differs from the one launched at an angle?
toLevel3.correct: The horizontal launch has no initial upward motion so the ball descends immediately
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A horizontal launch starts with zero vertical velocity, so the projectile begins falling right away rather than rising first.

distractors.answer: The horizontal launch follows a straight diagonal line
distractors.explanation: Both trajectories are parabolic; the horizontal launch just begins curving downward from the start.

distractors.answer: The angled launch has no horizontal velocity at all
distractors.explanation: An angled launch has both horizontal and vertical components of velocity.

distractors.answer: The horizontal launch is not affected by the gravitational force
distractors.explanation: The gravitational force acts on all projectiles regardless of their launch angle.

toLevel3.question: In projectile motion, the horizontal and vertical motions are described as independent. Which one of the following best describes what this means?
toLevel3.correct: Each component can be analysed separately without affecting the other
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The gravitational force affects only the vertical motion, and horizontal motion proceeds unchanged, so the two can be treated independently.

distractors.answer: The projectile can only move in one direction at a time
distractors.explanation: A projectile moves in both directions simultaneously; independence means the components do not influence each other.

distractors.answer: Horizontal motion stops when vertical motion begins
distractors.explanation: Both motions occur simultaneously throughout the flight.

distractors.answer: Vertical motion has no effect on the overall path
distractors.explanation: Vertical motion absolutely affects the path; independence means the two components do not affect each other.

toLevel3.question: Jo kicks a ball at an angle on flat ground. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following best describes why the descending half of the trajectory is a mirror image of the ascending half?
toLevel3.correct: Gravitational acceleration is constant and symmetric about the peak
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Constant downward acceleration produces equal changes in vertical velocity going up and coming down, creating a symmetric path.

distractors.answer: The ball travels at the same speed at every point on both halves
distractors.explanation: The total speed is not equal at every symmetric pair of points; horizontal velocity is constant but the vertical component reverses.

distractors.answer: The ball has the same height at launch and landing
distractors.explanation: Equal heights at start and end are a result of symmetry, not its cause.

distractors.answer: Wind pushes equally on both halves of the path
distractors.explanation: Symmetry arises from constant gravitational acceleration, not wind effects.

toLevel3.question: Anna observes a water jet from a garden hose following a curved path through the air. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following best describes why the water follows a curved path rather than a straight one?
toLevel3.correct: The gravitational force pulls the water downward while it moves forward
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The water has constant horizontal velocity from the hose, but the gravitational force accelerates it downward, creating a parabolic arc.

distractors.answer: Water pressure decreases as the jet travels further from the hose
distractors.explanation: Once the water leaves the hose, pressure is no longer relevant; the gravitational force shapes the curve.

distractors.answer: The water molecules decelerate due to cohesion forces within the jet
distractors.explanation: Cohesion does not cause the curved trajectory; the gravitational force is responsible.

distractors.answer: Air resistance bends the water jet downward
distractors.explanation: While air resistance has some effect, the primary cause of the curve is the gravitational acceleration.

toLevel3.question: A student claims: 'A projectile launched at an angle has the same horizontal velocity at the start and end of its flight when air resistance is ignored.' The student's claim is correct.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: With no horizontal force, the horizontal component of velocity remains constant throughout the entire trajectory.

distractors.explanation: Students may think the projectile decelerates overall, but the horizontal component specifically remains unchanged when air resistance is ignored.

toLevel3.prompt: Kate analyses the trajectory of a ball launched into the air. Ignore air resistance. Complete the sentence explaining why the trajectory is parabolic.
toLevel3.sentence: A parabolic trajectory results from combining {{blank:1}} horizontal motion with uniformly {{blank:2}} vertical motion.

1.correctExplanation: Horizontal velocity does not change because no horizontal force acts on the projectile.

distractors.explanation: There is no horizontal force, so horizontal motion is constant, not accelerating.
Without air resistance, no force acts to decelerate horizontal motion.

2.correctExplanation: The gravitational force provides a constant downward acceleration of 9.8 m s⁻², uniformly changing the vertical velocity.

distractors.explanation: Vertical velocity changes continuously due to the gravitational acceleration.
Vertical velocity changes steadily in one direction, not back and forth.

toLevel3.prompt: Liam analyses the symmetry of a projectile's trajectory on flat ground. Ignore air resistance. Complete the sentence.
toLevel3.sentence: The ascending and descending halves of a projectile's path are symmetric because gravitational {{blank:1}} is constant and the vertical velocity at any height is equal in {{blank:2}} on each side of the peak.

1.correctExplanation: The constant value of gravitational acceleration (9.8 m s⁻² downward) ensures the trajectory is symmetric.

distractors.explanation: Gravitational velocity is not a standard term; the constant quantity is gravitational acceleration.
While the gravitational force is constant for a given mass, the key physics concept here is constant acceleration.

2.correctExplanation: At the same height, the vertical speed is the same going up as going down, just in opposite directions.

distractors.explanation: The directions are opposite on each side; it is the magnitude that is equal.
Duration describes time, not the equality of speed values at matching heights.

toLevel3.prompt: Sam launches a ball horizontally from the edge of a cliff. Ignore air resistance. Complete the sentence about the ball's initial motion.
toLevel3.sentence: A projectile launched horizontally from a cliff begins with zero {{blank:1}} velocity, so it starts falling {{blank:2}} from the moment of release.

1.correctExplanation: A horizontal launch means all initial velocity is horizontal; the vertical velocity starts at zero.

distractors.explanation: A horizontal launch has nonzero horizontal velocity; it is the vertical component that starts at zero.
The total initial speed is not zero for a horizontal launch; only the vertical component is zero.

2.correctExplanation: With no initial upward velocity, the gravitational force begins pulling the projectile downward from the instant of release.

distractors.explanation: The projectile begins falling at the instant of release, not after a delay.
There is no delay; the gravitational force acts from the very first moment of flight.

toLevel4.question: Anna throws a ball horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ from the edge of a 20 m high cliff. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following is closest to the horizontal distance from the base of the cliff at which the ball lands?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Time to fall 20 m: t = √(2 × 20/9.8) = 2.02 s. Horizontal distance = 15 × 2.02 = 30.3 m, approximately 30 m.

distractors.explanation: This uses only the horizontal speed without correctly calculating the fall time from the height.
This overestimates the fall time or incorrectly doubles the horizontal distance.
This confuses the vertical drop distance with the horizontal range.

toLevel4.question: A ball is launched at 40 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Which one of the following is closest to the initial vertical component of the velocity?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: The vertical component = 40 × sin 30° = 40 × 0.5 = 20 m s⁻¹ upward.

distractors.explanation: This is the horizontal component (40 × cos 30°), not the vertical component.
40 m s⁻¹ is the total launch speed, not the vertical component alone.
This incorrectly halves the vertical component or uses the wrong trigonometric function.

toLevel4.question: Jo kicks a football at an angle above the horizontal. Ignore air resistance. At the highest point of its trajectory, which one of the following best describes the velocity of the football?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: At the peak, the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity remains unchanged, so only horizontal velocity exists.

distractors.explanation: Only the vertical velocity is zero at the peak; horizontal velocity remains constant throughout.
The vertical velocity is zero at the peak; the projectile retains its horizontal velocity.

distractors.answer: Its speed equals the launch speed
distractors.explanation: At the peak, the speed equals only the horizontal component, which is less than the full launch speed.

toLevel4.question: Kate releases two balls from the same height at the same instant: one is dropped vertically from rest and the other is thrown horizontally. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following best describes which ball hits the ground first?
toLevel4.correct: They hit the ground at the same time
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Both have the same initial vertical velocity (zero) and the same vertical acceleration (g), so they fall the same vertical distance in the same time.

distractors.explanation: The horizontal velocity of the thrown ball does not affect its vertical fall time.
Horizontal motion does not change the time taken to fall a given vertical distance.

distractors.answer: It depends on the horizontal speed of the thrown ball
distractors.explanation: Vertical and horizontal motions are independent; horizontal speed does not influence fall time.

toLevel4.question: A ball is launched at 25 m s⁻¹ at 60° above the horizontal. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following is closest to the speed of the ball at the highest point of its trajectory?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: At the peak, only horizontal velocity remains: vₓ = 25 × cos 60° = 25 × 0.5 = 12.5 m s⁻¹.

distractors.explanation: Only the vertical component is zero at the peak; the horizontal component of 12.5 m s⁻¹ persists.
25 m s⁻¹ is the launch speed; at the peak, the speed equals just the horizontal component.
This is the initial vertical component (25 × sin 60°), not the speed at the peak.

toLevel4.question: Liam throws a stone horizontally from a bridge. The stone takes 3.0 s to reach the water below. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following is closest to the vertical velocity of the stone just before it hits the water?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Vertical velocity = g × t = 9.8 × 3.0 = 29.4 m s⁻¹ downward, since the initial vertical velocity is zero.

distractors.explanation: 9.8 m s⁻² is the acceleration, not the final velocity after 3.0 s of falling.
44.1 m is the vertical distance fallen (½ × 9.8 × 9), not the velocity.
This uses half the correct time or incorrectly divides; v = 9.8 × 3.0 = 29.4 m s⁻¹.

toLevel4.question: A cannonball is fired at 50 m s⁻¹ at 45° above the horizontal. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following is closest to the maximum height reached by the cannonball?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Vertical component = 50 × sin 45° = 35.36 m s⁻¹. Maximum height = vᵧ²/(2g) = 35.36²/(2 × 9.8) = 1250/19.6 = 63.8 m.

distractors.explanation: This incorrectly uses the full launch speed instead of just the vertical component.
This halves the correct answer, perhaps from using an incorrect formula.
This results from a calculation error, not the correct application of v² = 2gh.

toLevel4.prompt: Ben throws a ball horizontally at 10 m s⁻¹ from the top of a 44.1 m high building. Ignore air resistance. Complete the calculation.
toLevel4.sentence: The ball takes {{blank:1}} seconds to reach the ground, landing {{blank:2}} m from the base of the building.

1.correctExplanation: Using h = ½gt²: 44.1 = ½ × 9.8 × t², so t² = 9.0, giving t = 3.0 s.

distractors.explanation: This incorrectly uses h = gt instead of h = ½gt².
This results from a calculation error in solving the displacement equation.

2.correctExplanation: Horizontal distance = horizontal speed × time = 10 × 3.0 = 30 m.

distractors.explanation: 44.1 m is the vertical height, not the horizontal distance.
10 m s⁻¹ is the horizontal speed, not the horizontal distance.

toLevel4.prompt: Jo launches a ball at 30 m s⁻¹ at 60° above the horizontal. Complete the calculation of the initial velocity components.
toLevel4.sentence: The ball has an initial horizontal velocity of {{blank:1}} m s⁻¹ and an initial vertical velocity of {{blank:2}} m s⁻¹.

distractors.explanation: 26 m s⁻¹ is the vertical component (30 × sin 60°), not the horizontal component.
30 m s⁻¹ is the total speed; the horizontal component requires multiplying by cos 60°.
15 m s⁻¹ is the horizontal component (30 × cos 60°), not the vertical component.
30 m s⁻¹ is the total speed; the vertical component requires multiplying by sin 60°.

toLevel4.prompt: Anna drops a stone from rest. Complete the calculation of the fall time and final speed.
toLevel4.sentence: A stone dropped from rest takes {{blank:1}} seconds to fall 19.6 m, reaching a final vertical speed of {{blank:2}} m s⁻¹.

1.correctExplanation: Using h = ½gt²: 19.6 = ½ × 9.8 × t², so t² = 4.0, giving t = 2.0 s.

distractors.explanation: In 1.0 s the stone falls only 4.9 m, not 19.6 m.
In 4.0 s the stone would fall 78.4 m, much further than 19.6 m.

2.correctExplanation: Final speed = g × t = 9.8 × 2.0 = 19.6 m s⁻¹.

distractors.explanation: 9.8 m s⁻¹ is the speed after 1.0 s, not after 2.0 s.
This doubles the correct value, as if using t = 4.0 s.

toLevel5.question: A student claims that a projectile is in equilibrium at the peak of its trajectory because its vertical velocity is zero. Which one of the following best describes the evaluation of this claim?
toLevel5.correct: The claim is incorrect because a net downward gravitational force still acts, so the projectile is not in equilibrium
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Equilibrium requires zero net force. The gravitational force acts on the projectile at all times, including at the peak where the vertical velocity is momentarily zero.

distractors.answer: The claim is correct because zero vertical velocity means zero net force
distractors.explanation: Zero velocity does not mean zero force; the gravitational force provides a constant unbalanced force downward.

distractors.answer: The claim is correct because the projectile is momentarily stationary at the peak
distractors.explanation: The projectile still has horizontal velocity at the peak and an unbalanced gravitational force.

distractors.answer: The claim is incorrect, but only because horizontal velocity exists at the peak
distractors.explanation: Equilibrium depends on net force being zero, not velocity; the key issue is that the gravitational force still acts.

toLevel5.question: Two projectiles are launched at the same speed on flat ground: one at 30° above the horizontal and one at 60° above the horizontal. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following best describes the comparison of their horizontal ranges?
toLevel5.correct: They have equal ranges because complementary angles produce the same range
toLevel5.correctExplanation: For the same launch speed on level ground, angles that sum to 90° produce identical horizontal ranges because sin(2 × 30°) = sin(2 × 60°).

distractors.explanation: While 30° has greater horizontal velocity, 60° has longer flight time; the ranges are equal.
While 60° reaches higher altitude, 30° covers more ground per second; the ranges are equal.

distractors.answer: The range depends only on launch speed, not angle
distractors.explanation: Range depends on both speed and angle; complementary angles happen to give equal range.

toLevel5.question: A student analyses the trajectory of a golf ball and observes that it deviates from the ideal parabolic path. Which one of the following best describes the most significant factor causing this deviation?
toLevel5.correct: Air resistance reduces horizontal velocity and changes the trajectory shape
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Air resistance provides a force opposing motion, reducing horizontal velocity over time and making the descent steeper than the ascent.

distractors.answer: The gravitational acceleration increases during the flight of the ball
distractors.explanation: Gravitational acceleration is effectively constant over the distances a golf ball travels.

distractors.answer: The ball's mass decreases as it travels through air
distractors.explanation: A golf ball's mass does not change during flight.

distractors.answer: Earth's rotation deflects the ball during its flight
distractors.explanation: While the Coriolis effect exists, it is negligible for golf ball distances compared to air resistance.

toLevel5.question: In an experiment, Sam drops Ball A from rest and simultaneously fires Ball B horizontally from the same height. Ignore air resistance. Both balls hit the ground at the same time. Which one of the following best describes what this demonstrates about the independence of motion components?
toLevel5.correct: Horizontal motion does not influence the rate of vertical fall
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Since both balls fall the same vertical distance in the same time, horizontal velocity has no effect on vertical acceleration.

distractors.answer: The horizontal ball experiences a greater gravitational force
distractors.explanation: Both balls have the same gravitational acceleration regardless of horizontal motion.

distractors.answer: The gravitational force only acts on objects that are stationary horizontally
distractors.explanation: The gravitational force acts equally on all objects regardless of their horizontal velocity.

distractors.answer: The experiment would not work outside a vacuum chamber
distractors.explanation: The result is visible in air; air resistance slightly affects timing but the principle holds.

toLevel5.question: A student argues that since a projectile decelerates on the way up and accelerates on the way down, there must be two different forces acting during the flight. Which one of the following best describes the evaluation of this reasoning?
toLevel5.correct: Only one force acts: the gravitational force decelerates upward motion and accelerates downward motion
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The gravitational force is the sole force throughout. It opposes upward velocity (causing deceleration) and enhances downward velocity (causing acceleration), but it is the same constant force.

distractors.answer: The student is correct that two forces are required
distractors.explanation: A single constant downward force explains both the deceleration upward and acceleration downward.

distractors.answer: There are zero forces at the peak between the two phases
distractors.explanation: The gravitational force acts continuously, including at the peak; there is no force-free moment.

distractors.answer: A third force at the peak switches between the two phases
distractors.explanation: No switching mechanism exists; the gravitational force is one constant downward force throughout.

toLevel5.question: For a projectile launched on level ground, a launch angle of 45° gives the maximum horizontal range. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following best describes why 45° provides the optimal balance?
toLevel5.correct: It maximises the product of horizontal velocity and flight time
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Range = horizontal velocity × flight time. At 45°, the product of cos θ and sin θ is maximised, giving the greatest range.

distractors.answer: It minimises the effect of the gravitational force on the projectile
distractors.explanation: Gravitational acceleration is the same regardless of launch angle; 45° optimises the velocity split.

distractors.answer: It produces the longest possible flight time overall
distractors.explanation: A 90° launch gives the longest flight time; 45° balances time and horizontal speed.

distractors.answer: It gives the highest horizontal velocity component
distractors.explanation: A 0° launch gives maximum horizontal velocity; 45° balances both components.

toLevel5.question: Data from a projectile experiment shows the landing point is significantly short of the predicted range. The launch speed and angle were measured correctly. Which one of the following best describes the most likely explanation?
toLevel5.correct: Air resistance reduced the horizontal velocity during flight
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Air resistance acts opposite to motion, decelerating the horizontal velocity and reducing the actual range below the theoretical prediction.

distractors.answer: The gravitational field strength was stronger than 9.8 m s⁻² on that day
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field strength does not vary significantly at a given location from day to day.

distractors.answer: The projectile gained mass during its flight path
distractors.explanation: The projectile mass does not increase during flight; air resistance is the primary cause.

distractors.answer: The launch angle was actually greater than the measured value
distractors.explanation: The problem states the angle was correct; the shortfall is due to air resistance.

toLevel5.question: Kate compares the acceleration vectors of a projectile at three points during its flight: just after launch, at the peak, and just before landing. Ignore air resistance. Which one of the following best describes the pattern?
toLevel5.correct: All three acceleration vectors are identical in magnitude and direction
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Gravitational acceleration is constant at 9.8 m s⁻² downward at every point in the trajectory, regardless of position or velocity.

distractors.answer: Acceleration is upward after launch, zero at the peak, and downward before landing
distractors.explanation: Acceleration is always 9.8 m s⁻² downward; it never points upward or becomes zero.

distractors.answer: Acceleration increases as the projectile descends
distractors.explanation: Gravitational acceleration remains constant at 9.8 m s⁻² regardless of height changes over these distances.

distractors.answer: Acceleration is largest at the peak where velocity is lowest
distractors.explanation: Acceleration does not depend on velocity; it is constant at 9.8 m s⁻² downward throughout.

toLevel5.prompt: Ben analyses the relationship between launch angle and range on flat ground. Ignore air resistance. Complete the sentence.
toLevel5.sentence: Maximum range on flat ground occurs at {{blank:1}}° because this angle maximises the product of {{blank:2}} velocity and flight time.

1.correctExplanation: At 45°, sin(2 × 45°) = sin 90° = 1, which maximises the range formula R = v² sin(2θ)/g.

distractors.explanation: 60° gives a longer flight time but lower horizontal velocity, resulting in less range than 45°.
30° gives greater horizontal velocity but shorter flight time, resulting in less range than 45°.

2.correctExplanation: Range equals horizontal velocity multiplied by total flight time; 45° optimises this product.

distractors.explanation: Vertical velocity determines height and flight time, but range depends on horizontal velocity multiplied by time.
Terminal velocity is related to air resistance, not the range optimisation of projectile motion.

toLevel5.prompt: Anna evaluates the effect of air resistance on projectile motion. Complete the sentence.
toLevel5.sentence: Air resistance makes a real projectile's trajectory {{blank:1}} compared to the ideal parabola, because the {{blank:2}} half of the path is steeper than the ascending half.

1.correctExplanation: Air resistance reduces horizontal velocity over time, making the descending path steeper and the trajectory no longer a perfect parabola.

distractors.explanation: Air resistance breaks the symmetry by reducing speed throughout the flight, especially in the horizontal direction.
Air resistance does not produce a circular path; it creates an asymmetric curve steeper on descent.

2.correctExplanation: By the descending phase, air resistance has reduced horizontal velocity, so the projectile drops more steeply.

distractors.explanation: The ascending half is less affected; cumulative velocity loss makes the descending half steeper.
The horizontal portion is not a distinct phase; the trajectory becomes steeper on the way down.
